title: Understanding Progressive Collapse: How To Avoid A Cascading Failure
gist: Sam Newman maps 'progressive collapse' from civil engineering (the 1968 Ronan Point tower failure) onto distributed systems, using the AWS us-east-1 DNS race-condition outage and a used-car site's connection-pool exhaustion to argue that resilience requires reducing hazards, strengthening components, and reducing interconnection, while warning that added redundancy and circuit breakers can themselves introduce new failure modes.

themes.theme: Progressive collapse as a resilience lens

insights.claim: Progressive collapse is defined as a situation where a small, innocent-looking initial failure cascades into a much larger collapse of the wider system, a concept borrowed from civil engineering (the 1968 Ronan Point tower failure) and directly applicable to reasoning about distributed system outages.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: Gives architects and SREs a reusable mental model for postmortems: look for the small trigger that a system had no way to contain before it grew.
insights.quote: A progressive collapse describes a situation where a small failure results in a significant collapse in the wider system.
insights.locator: Examples of Progressive Collapses

insights.claim: The Ronan Point tower collapse traced back to lower-skilled construction workers substituting improper materials (newspaper and cigarette packets instead of concrete) to join prefabricated panels during a rushed post-war housing boom, a defect only discovered years later through forensic deconstruction of the building.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A template for technical-debt risk: shortcuts taken to build fast under skill or time constraints can remain invisible until a much later, unrelated trigger exposes them.
insights.locator: 2. Strengthen Components

insights.claim: Newman draws an explicit parallel between the 1960s use of lower-skilled labor to build high-rise housing faster (which caused Ronan Point) and today's use of AI coding agents combined with reduced junior-developer hiring, framing both as the same trade-off of speed versus verified quality.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A caution flag for engineering leaders cutting junior headcount while scaling AI-generated code: the historical analogue ended in a fatal structural failure that took over a decade to fully explain.
insights.quote: We're doing that by getting rid of junior developers and not hiring M&Es.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: The AWS us-east-1 outage was caused by a race condition in DynamoDB's DNS-automation subsystem: a slow-to-complete DNS 'plan' was superseded by a newer plan from a different DNS 'enactor' instance, and when the stale plan finally finished executing it wiped out the correct, newer DNS routes in Route 53.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A concrete failure mechanism (stale-write-wins race condition in automated DNS orchestration) worth checking for in any team's own control-plane automation.
insights.locator: Let's talk about what happened with AWS

insights.claim: The root cause of the AWS DNS race condition was the redundancy itself: running multiple DNS enactor instances for resiliency is what allowed two plans to execute out of order; a single enactor would have processed plans sequentially and the race condition could not have occurred.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: Redundancy is not unconditionally safer — it can create new correlated failure modes, so teams should audit whether 'more instances for resilience' introduces race conditions rather than removing risk.
insights.locator: Think about the AWS outage

insights.claim: The AWS outage cascaded broadly because many downstream AWS services (network load balancers, compute, queueing, EKS) depend on the same DNS/routing layer, ultimately taking down customer-facing products including Amazon's own Alexa, plus Ring, Slack, Snapchat, Zoom, and Shopify.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: Illustrates concentration risk from shared dependence on a single cloud region's control plane — relevant to assessing vendor and customer exposure to us-east-1.
insights.locator: This in turn had a cascading effect

insights.claim: AWS's immediate post-incident remediation was to disable the automated DNS management system entirely as a fail-safe while adding stronger pre-production testing, rather than attempting to patch the race condition live.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A model 'reduce hazards' response: cut the automated capability first, harden it later, rather than risk shipping a fix mid-incident.
insights.locator: What about AWS?

insights.claim: A legacy used-vehicle marketplace application ('Sauron'), mid-migration under the Strangler Fig pattern and running on 10 servers, collapsed when concurrent requests spiked from a normal 30-60 to over 800, because a downstream legacy site began hanging on connections instead of failing, and a lenient 30-second timeout let the shared connection pool — then the OS thread pool — become fully exhausted.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A concrete architecture-review checklist item: audit shared connection pools and timeout settings for any Java-style native-threading service calling flaky downstream dependencies.
insights.locator: What happened with the used car site?

insights.claim: User behavior amplified the used-car site's collapse: as pages hung, users repeatedly hit refresh, generating more concurrent requests and accelerating exhaustion of the connection and thread pools in a feedback loop.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A reminder that client retry/refresh behavior under stress is itself a load-amplification hazard that resilience designs must account for, not just backend logic.
insights.locator: This was made worse because when the website hung

insights.claim: In hindsight, adding load shedding — capping concurrent request handling at the system's known safe capacity and dropping excess requests — would have kept the used-car site running instead of collapsing entirely, but the team chose not to invest in strengthening the legacy component because it was near retirement and represented only a fraction of business revenue.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A prioritization framework: cheap load-shedding guardrails are worth adding even on components not worth deeper investment, since they cap downside without requiring a full rewrite.
insights.locator: What I found out about years later

themes.theme: Mitigation framework and the root-cause fallacy

insights.claim: Newman synthesizes a three-part framework for mitigating progressive collapse — drawn from a 216-page NIST report on building collapse processed via NotebookLM — of reducing hazards, strengthening components, and reducing interconnection, and argues it is directly portable to distributed-system design reviews.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A usable three-item checklist teams can apply to their own resilience reviews rather than a vague call to 'be more resilient.'
insights.locator: In that spirit, what can we do to mitigate a progressive collapse?

insights.claim: Newman argues that fixating on a single 'root cause' is misleading for complex systems, citing wildfire management — where controls like banning open fires and clearing brush reduce risk without eliminating all ignition sources like lightning — as the model resilience engineering should follow instead of traditional safety management's goal of preventing all bad events.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: Reframes incident response strategy: budget for layered mitigations against a class of failures rather than chasing a single fix for 'the' root cause.
insights.quote: I want to preface this by saying that focusing on a single root cause is highly problematic.
insights.locator: How to Mitigate a Progressive Collapse

insights.claim: Multi-region disaster-recovery options form a cost/complexity spectrum — backup-and-restore, pilot light, warm standby, and full active-active multi-site — where downtime and data-loss windows shrink but cost and operational complexity rise at each step.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A baseline mental model for evaluating whether a company's DR spend matches its actual downtime/data-loss tolerance.
insights.locator: You've then got variations, the warm failover

insights.claim: Newman is skeptical of multi-cloud as a default best practice, arguing it multiplies operational complexity by requiring expertise across multiple providers (or a commoditized abstraction like Kubernetes) without removing risk, since deploying identical code across vendors relocates the interconnection risk into the shared codebase — a bug that fails on AWS can just as easily fail on Azure.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the post-outage Hacker News reflex of 'just go multi-cloud' — worth weighing against the specific vendor-failure risk being hedged, not applied as a blanket rule.
insights.quote: If you deploy the same code in vendor A as you do in vendor B, your code itself is a form of interconnection.
insights.locator: What about multi-cloud?

insights.claim: Most major companies affected by the AWS us-east-1 outage had deliberately chosen not to run hot multi-region failover, largely for cost reasons, since region-level failures are rare — a conscious trade-off rather than an oversight.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: Frames post-outage 'why weren't they multi-region' criticism as often a rational cost decision, useful context when evaluating a vendor's resilience posture after an incident.
insights.locator: Why weren't more of those big-name companies running a multi-site setup?

insights.claim: Monzo, under UK banking-license continuity-of-service requirements, built a clean-room re-implementation of its core banking functionality with no shared code, running on GCP alongside its primary AWS-hosted system, specifically to hedge both vendor-failure risk and the risk of a shared code bug propagating across sites.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A concrete, regulator-driven precedent for genuine interconnection reduction beyond routine multi-region replication — relevant to fintech resilience and regulatory-compliance posture.
insights.locator: We can look at someone like Monzo

themes.theme: Reducing interconnection and the resilience-complexity paradox

insights.claim: Bulkheads (the shipping-derived compartmentalization pattern) translate to software as per-dependency connection-pool isolation; the used-car site retrofitted ring-fenced connection pools per downstream service after its incident, and circuit breakers act as an on-demand trigger for the same bulkhead effect.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A concrete implementation pattern (per-dependency pool isolation) teams can retrofit without a full rewrite, as demonstrated in the article's own case study.
insights.locator: What about with our used car site?

insights.claim: Circuit breakers are not a free resilience win: Newman warns, citing Marc Brooker, that they can worsen partial failure (a failing endpoint trips the breaker for functioning endpoints too) and cause 'boom and bust' retry storms when many clients trip and re-flood simultaneously, recommending they be scoped to retries only or replaced with token buckets.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A concrete red flag for architecture reviews: audit circuit-breaker configuration for retry-storm risk rather than assuming they are a default safe addition.
insights.quote: Actually, adding circuit breakers can make other problems worse.
insights.locator: There are a bunch of issues around circuit breakers

insights.claim: Adding resilience mechanisms (redundancy, circuit breakers, multi-cloud) can itself increase system complexity to the point of introducing new failure modes — Newman cites David Woods' research framing this as a largely unsolvable tension, meaning teams must consciously decline certain resilience patterns rather than assume more machinery is always safer.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive guidance for infrastructure investment: complexity-driven resilience spend has diminishing, and sometimes negative, returns past a point — worth factoring into build-vs-skip decisions on new resilience tooling.
insights.locator: This is something that David Woods has talked about a lot

insights.claim: Newman argues that publicly published incident reports (AWS's, Cloudflare's) function simultaneously as PR and as genuine industry-wide learning tools, and singles out Cloudflare's reports as unusually self-critical and detailed compared to peers.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A usable signal for evaluating vendor transparency and operational maturity: the candor of a company's public postmortems is itself informative.
insights.locator: The Importance of Learning from Incidents

themes.theme: AI agents and the future of QA

insights.claim: Newman predicts renewed demand for dedicated QA and SRE roles as a guardrail against AI-generated code, arguing the 'shift-left' trend that eliminated dedicated QA was premature, and that the industry now needs technical QAs able to verify system properties and outputs of AI-generated code rather than relying on developers to self-review.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A hiring and product signal: watch for renewed demand in QA/SRE roles and for tooling that supports independent verification of AI-written code as a growth category.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers

insights.claim: Newman frames the AI-coding-agent guardrail problem using the same two-part lens as Ronan Point: whether the underlying system (model) is good enough, and whether it was correctly implemented and verified — arguing the industry is 'not nowhere near' having good enough verification standards yet.
insights.speaker: Sam Newman
insights.so_what: A structured way to evaluate AI-coding-agent risk in production: separate model-quality risk from verification-process risk, and don't assume progress on one solves the other.
insights.locator: Questions and Answers
